title: Neonatal sepsis
subject: paediatrics
setting: SNCU, NICU, postnatal ward, primary care (young infants 0 to 59 days)
summary: Suspect sepsis in any unwell neonate; take a blood culture and start ampicillin plus gentamicin (WHO 2024 first choice; NNF for SNCUs), escalating by local antibiogram in NICUs. Do an LP when meningitis is possible. Stop at 36 hours if culture is sterile and the baby is well; treat culture-positive sepsis 10 to 14 days and meningitis at least 21 days.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Early-onset sepsis (EOS) starts before 72 hours of life and late-onset sepsis (LOS) at 72 hours or later; in India organisms and resistance often overlap between the two.

WHO signs of suspected sepsis (0 to 59 days, hospital): not feeding well, movement only when stimulated or none, temperature 38 °C or more or below 35.5 °C, severe chest indrawing, convulsions, fast breathing (60/min or more) at 0 to 6 days, drowsiness, grunting, central cyanosis, severe jaundice, severe abdominal distension.
Suspect meningitis with drowsiness or lethargy, convulsions, bulging fontanelle, irritability or high-pitched cry; neck stiffness is rare in young infants.

EOS risk factors (NNF 2021). Red flags: clinical chorioamnionitis, foul-smelling liquor. Yellow flags: preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, rupture of membranes for 18 hours or more, intrapartum fever of 38 °C or more with suspected infection, unclean delivery or cord care.
Suspected staphylococcal infection: sepsis signs plus skin pustules, omphalitis or abscesses.

sections.title: Start treatment
items: Stabilise airway, breathing and circulation; correct hypoglycaemia and hypothermia. Treat shock early with a senior, avoiding repeated blind fluid boluses (especially in preterm babies) and starting vasoactive support early.
Take a blood culture of adequate volume before the first antibiotic dose, but do not delay antibiotics for a difficult culture or lumbar puncture.

Symptomatic neonates of any gestation with perinatal risk factors: start antibiotics. Asymptomatic babies below 35 weeks with risk factors: consider antibiotics (over 32 weeks, 1 red or 2 yellow flags; 32 weeks or less, 1 red or 1 yellow flag). Asymptomatic babies of 35 weeks or more: observe and treat only if sepsis markers are abnormal (NNF 2021).
First choice (WHO 2024; NNF recommends it for SNCUs over cefotaxime plus amikacin): ampicillin plus gentamicin IV or IM. Use cloxacillin in place of ampicillin for suspected staphylococcal sepsis.

Level III NICUs with high resistance: choose empirical therapy from the unit antibiogram and escalate only for clinical deterioration or proven resistance; reserve carbapenems and colistin for proven or highly likely resistant infection.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Blood culture in all before antibiotics. NNF advises against routine CRP for diagnosing late-onset sepsis (it may be used to help rule out sepsis in level 2 units without culture facilities); procalcitonin offers no advantage over CRP.

Lumbar puncture: in culture-positive sepsis, clinical signs of meningitis, most late-onset sepsis once stable, and sepsis not responding to treatment. Defer while unstable but start antibiotics. Use CSF cell count and protein rather than glucose to diagnose meningitis.
Urine culture (suprapubic or catheter sample) in late-onset sepsis; chest X-ray for respiratory signs; glucose, blood gas and CBC with platelets.

sections.title: Duration and de-escalation
items: Started for suspected EOS: stop at 36 hours if the blood culture is sterile, the baby is stable and there are no signs of sepsis (NNF).

Probable (culture-negative) sepsis or pneumonia: 5 to 7 days IV (NNF); WHO 2024 advises at least 7 days for pneumonia and at least 10 days for suspected sepsis in hospital. Do not stop early on the basis of negative biomarkers alone.

Culture-positive uncomplicated sepsis: 10 to 14 days. Meningitis: at least 21 days (ampicillin or cefotaxime or ceftriaxone plus gentamicin); complicated meningitis (ventriculitis, abscess): 4 to 6 weeks. Uncomplicated UTI: about 14 days.
Candidaemia: antifungal for 14 days after documented clearance from the blood and resolution of signs; longer for deep-seated infection.
Narrow therapy as soon as culture and sensitivity results are available.

sections.title: Where referral is not possible (WHO 2024 PSBI)
items: Critical illness (not able to feed at all, no movement, or convulsions): refer; if referral is impossible give ampicillin plus gentamicin IM or IV for at least 10 days.

Clinical severe infection (not feeding well, movement only when stimulated, fever or hypothermia, severe chest indrawing, or fast breathing at 0 to 6 days): refer; if not possible give oral amoxicillin for at least 7 days plus gentamicin IM or IV for 7 days (2 days if 7 is not feasible).
Fast breathing as the only sign: at 0 to 6 days refer (oral amoxicillin for 7 days if referral is impossible); at 7 to 59 days treat at home with oral amoxicillin for at least 7 days.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: Monitor temperature, perfusion, heart rate, apnoea, glucose, feeding and urine output; repeat blood culture if persistently positive or not improving.
Measure gentamicin levels where possible, particularly in preterm infants and renal impairment, and extend the dosing interval if the trough is high.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Using third-generation cephalosporins with amikacin or carbapenems as routine first line in SNCUs, which drives resistance.
Continuing antibiotics for days despite a sterile culture and a well baby.
Missing meningitis because an LP was never done.
Using ceftriaxone in jaundiced neonates or with IV calcium-containing fluids; prefer cefotaxime.

drugs.name: Ampicillin
drugs.dose: 50 mg/kg per dose IV or IM every 12 hours in the first week of life, every 8 hours after the first week
drugs.notes: First choice with gentamicin; duration by diagnosis.

drugs.name: Gentamicin
drugs.dose: 5 mg/kg IV or IM once daily in the first week of life; 7.5 mg/kg once daily after the first week
drugs.notes: WHO 2024 doses. In preterm babies or renal impairment, use unit formulary intervals and trough levels.

drugs.name: Cloxacillin
drugs.dose: 50 mg/kg per dose IV or IM every 12 hours in the first week, every 8 hours after the first week
drugs.notes: Replaces ampicillin for suspected staphylococcal sepsis or pneumonia.

drugs.name: Cefotaxime
drugs.dose: 50 mg/kg per dose IV every 12 hours in the first week, every 6 hours after the first week
drugs.notes: Meningitis, with gentamicin, for at least 3 weeks; preferred over ceftriaxone in jaundiced neonates.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.dose: 100 mg/kg IV or IM once daily
drugs.notes: Meningitis alternative; avoid with hyperbilirubinaemia or IV calcium.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin (oral)
drugs.dose: 50 mg/kg per dose every 12 hours in the first week of life, every 8 hours after the first week
drugs.notes: WHO outpatient PSBI regimens; for fast breathing alone, 50 mg/kg every 12 hours for 7 days.
